la:verb:doleo.html:
dŏlĕo, ŭi, ĭtum (doliturus, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. also under !*?), 2, v. n. and a.
[perh. root in Sansc. dar-, dal-, to tear apart; cf. Gr. δέρω, to flay; Ger. zehren, to consume; Eng. tear].
Corporeally, to feel pain, suffer pain, be in pain, to ache: nequeo caput Tollere, ita dolui, itaque ego nunc doleo, etc.,; : doleo ab animo, doleo ab oculis, doleo ab aegritudine,: si cor dolet, et si jecur, aut pulmones, aut praecordia,; cf.: pes, oculi, caput, latera, pulmones,: caput,; cf.: caput a sole,: renes,: hirae omnes,: oculi,: pes aegri,: dens,: uterum, et saep.: misero nunc malae dolent,; cf. : non metuo, ne quid mihi doleat, quod ferias,.—Esp., of the pangs of childbirth: Lucina dolentibus Juno dicta puerperis,.—With acc. of part affected (late Lat.): graviter oculos dolui,: doluisse te inguina cognosco, Marc. Aur. Ep. ad M. .—Impers.: mihi dolet, quom ego vapulo, ; cf. : si stimulos pugnis caedis, manibus plus dolet,.
Mentally.
Of personal subjects, to grieve for, deplore, lament, be sorry for, be afflicted at or on account of any thing (so most freq. and class.).
With acc.: meum casum luctumque doluerunt,; so, casum,; : Dionis mortem,: vicem alicujus,; ; ; fin.; : injurias alicujus, Cael. ap. : aliquid,; ; ; et saep. —
With acc. and inf.: inferiores non dolere (debent), se a suis superari,; ; ; ; ; ; ; et saep. —With simple inf.: vinci,. —
With abl.: laetari bonis rebus et dolere contrariis,: qua (epistola) lecta de Atticae febricula valde dolui,: delicto (opp. gaudere correctione),: laude aliena,: clade accepta,: injuriis civitatis suae,: dolore alicujus,: mea virtute,: laeso Metello,: quibus negatis,: successu,: Hercule deo,: rapto Ganymede, et saep.—
With de or ex: de Hortensio te certo scio dolere,; ; ; : quo gravius homines ex commutatione rerum doleant,; cf.: tum ex me doluisti,; and: EX QVO (sc. filio) NIHIL VNQVAM DOLVIT NISE CVM IS NON FVIT,.—(ε) With quod, quia, or si: doluisse se, quod populi Romani beneficium sibi extorqueretur,; ; cf. : doleo, quia doles et angere, Luccei. ap. : doliturus, si placeant spe deterius nostra,; cf. .—(ζ) Absol.: ah! nescis quam doleam,: et desperant et dolent et novissime oderunt,; ; ; ; et saep.: pars dolere pro gloria imperi, Kritz.; cf. .—So, dolentes, the mourners, .—
Of subjects not personal, to pain one (rare and mostly ante-class.).
With dat.: animus mihi dolet,; Phr. Caput mihi condoluit. Str. Quid mihi futurum'st, quoi duae ancillae dolent, i. e. are a painful subject, : dolet illud huic quod, etc.,; ; ; ; ; .— Impers., it pains me, I am grieved, I grieve.
With dat.: CONDISCES (i. e. condiscens = condiscipulus) CVI DOLET PRO AFRICANO, Corp. Inscr. L. 1, 2258 a: mihi dolebit, non tibi, si quid ego stulte fecero,; ; Caecil. ap. ; cf. prov.: cui dolet meminit, Anglice,the burnt child dreads the fire,.—
With acc. personae: frigida Eoo me dolet aura gelu,.—
Absol.: dolet (sc. mihi) dictum,: nec dolent prava,.—!*? Pass. as deponent: DE QVA NIHIL ALIVD DOLITVS EST (vir) NISI MORTEM,, and 794, 2: DOLEATVR,.—Hence, dŏlens, entis, P. a., causing pain, painful: nil dolentius,.—More freq., adv.: dŏlen-ter, painfully, with pain, with sorrow: dolenter hoc dicam potius quam contumeliose,; ; ; ; Planc. ap. ; — Comp., .—Sup. does not occur.

dŏcĕo, cŭi, ctum, 2, v. a.
root da; Zend. dā, to know; strengthened, dak-; Gr. διδάσκω; Lat. disco
,
to teach, instruct, inform, show, tell, etc. (for syn. cf.: edoceo, perdoceo, erudio, praecipio, instituo).
In gen., with double acc. of person and thing: pejor magister te istaec docuit ... illa, quae te docui,: hunc hominem cursuram,: aliquem artem,: aliquem litteras,: aliquem ejusmodi rem,: pueros elementa, et saep.—Pass., with acc. rei: is reliqua frustra docetur,; ; ; 6, 2, 3; ; et saep.; cf.: doctus dogmam, Laber. ap. P.; and: doctus militiam, ed. Gerl.—With inf.: docemur auctoritate domitas habere libidines,; ; : docemur disputare, non vivere (= discimus),: equi variare gyros docentur,; ; ; .—With acc. pers. and inf.: ut doceam Rullum posthac in iis saltem tacere rebus, in quibus, etc.,; so ; ; ; cf. ellipt. with abl. of instrument: Socratem fidibus (sc. canere),: aliquem docendum curare equo, armisque,; Zumpt, § 391 fin.—With acc. pers. and de, to instruct or inform one of: de ejus injuriis judices docere,: aliquem de aliqua re,; ; ; —With acc. pers. and rel. clause: doceant eum, qui vir Sex. Roscius fuerit,; ; ; ; —With acc. pers.: studiosos discendi erudiunt atque docent,; ; ; ; ; et saep.—With acc. rei: coepit studiose omnia Docere, educare, ita uti si esset filia,; so, aliquid,; ; ; et saep.; cf. also: quod de lacu Albano docuisset,; so with two acc., ; .—With acc. and inf.: docui per litteras, id nec opus esse nec fieri posse,; ; ; ; et saep.—Absol.: cum doceo et explano,; ; ; et saep.; cf. also: Tyrannio docet apud me,
In partic.: fabulam, like the Gr. διδάσκειν, qs. to teach a play to the actors, to rehearse; hence, to produce, exhibiton the stage: minor fuit aliquanto is, qui primus fabulam dedit, quam ii, qui multas docuerant (Plautus et Naevius),; ; ; .—Hence, doctus, a, um, P. a., learned, skilled, versed, experienced in any thing (cf.: litteratus, eruditus, peritus, gnarus, scitus).—Absol.: doctus vir et Graecis litteris eruditus,; cf. ; : adolescentes humanissimi et doctissimi,.—With ex: fuit enim doctus ex disciplina Stoicorum,.—With abl.: docti et Graecis litteris et Latinis,; fin.; ; . —With adv.: nec minus Graece quam Latine doctus,.—With gen.: fandi doctissima Cymodocea,: legum atque morum populi Romani jurisque civilis,: sagittarum,: artis lanificae,.—With acc.: (Maecenas) docte sermones utriusque linguae,: dulces modos (with citharae sciens),: omnia,: litteras,.—With inf.: doctus sagittas tendere Sericas,; ; ; et saep.—With ad or in: ad delinquendum doctior,: in parum fausto carmine docta fui,: Sapphica puella Musa doctior,more skilled in song,: docta puella,; (3, 2, 6 M.); 2, 13, 11 (3, 4, 11 M.).—Esp. as epithet of Catullus by other poets,; : Verona docti syllabas amat vatis,; .—As subst.: doctus, the man of skill.—Prov.: doctus in se semper divitias habet,; but class. only in plur.: doctī, ōrum, m., the learned: doctorum est ista consuetudo, et saep.—
Of things as subjects: frontes,: tibia, (3, 28, 16 M.): carmina,; cf. vox,: voces Pythagoreorum,: sermo,: prece,: manus artificis,; cf. ; ; : falx, (3, 12, 12 M.) et saep.—
In Plaut. and Ter., knowing, cunning, shrewd, subtle: malum, callidum, doctum,; ; ; et saep.; ; ; cf. also, dolus,; —docte, adv.
Learnedly, skilfully (very rare; not in Cic.).— Comp., ; .—Sup., .—
Cunningly, shrewdly, cleverly: docte et sapienter dicis,: docte tibi illam perdoctam dabo,; : docte sapere,; et saep.—Comp., .

dŏlor, ōris, m.
doleo

Mental, as a general designation of every painful, oppressive feeling, pain, distress, grief, tribulation, affliction, sorrow, anguish, trouble, vexation, mortification, chagrin, etc. (syn. luctus): dolor (est) aegritudo crucians,: si cadit in sapientem animi dolor,: quanta est cura in animo, quantum corde capio dolorem,; so with cura,: in labore atque in dolore,: majorem laetitiam ex desiderio bonorum percepimus, quam ex laetitia improborum dolorem,; cf. opp. laetatio,: te dolorem, quem acceperis cum summi viri tum amicissimi morte, ferre moderate,; cf. ; and: magno esse Germanis dolori Ariovisti mortem,; cf. also : magnum et acerbum dolorem commovere,: dolore angi,; cf. . —
Esp., indignation, wrath, animosity, anger, resentment: sed ego in hac sententia dicenda non parebo dolori meo, non iracundiae serviam,; cf. : et rei publicae injuriam et suum dolorem condonare,: qui accipit injuriam, et meminit et prae se fert dolorem suum,: magno dolore affici,; cf. fin.; ; cf. also: in eas (naves) indiligentiae suae ac doloris iracundia erupit,: quis indomitas tantus dolor excitat iras?; ; : amator agit ubi secum, Accedam? an potius mediter finire dolores,the torments of love,; cf. ; ; (4, 20, 17 M.) et saep.: Catonem veteres inimicitiae Caesaris incitant et dolor repulsae,; so, repulsae,: injuriae,: ignominiae,: conjugis amissae, et saep.: justus mihi dolor etiam adversus deos esset, quod, etc.,.—Prov.: dolorem longa consumit dies,; cf.: dolor decrescit, ubi quo crescat non habet, (Rib.).—
Terror, .—
Meton.
A grief, i. e. an object or cause of grief: illa (potest) etiam duris mentibus esse dolor,; .—
In rhet. lang. for the Gr. πάθος, passionate, warm expression; pathos, ; ; ; ; .

: insularum,: equi, et saep.—

Tarquinio) dominus exstiterit? hic est enim dominus populi, quem Graeci tyrannum vocant, etc.,; cf. ; .— Trop.: liberatos se per eum dicunt gravissimis dominis, terrore sempiterno ac nocturno metu,; of the judge: qui rei dominus futurus est,; poët. of the possessor of an art, ; .—
Poet., sometimes as an adj.: dominae manus,: arae,: praebere caput domina venale sub hasta,the auction spear,.—
In partic.
With or without convivii or epuli, the master of a feast, the entertainer, host, ; Lucil., Varr., and Sall. ap. ; Varr. ap. ; —
The master of a play or of public games; the employer of players or gladiators: quae mihi atque vobis res vortat bene Gregique huic et dominis atque conductoribus,; .—
In the period of the empire (Augustus and Tiberius declined it, ; ), a title of the emperors, ; ; ; ; ; —
A term of endearment in addressing a lover, .—
In respectful greeting, like our Sir, ; ; .—
A master or assignee of a forfeited estate, .—
Of Christ, the Lord (eccl. Lat.): Augusti Caesaris temporibus natus est Dominus Christus,; et saep.

do, dĕdi, dătum, dăre (also in a longer form, dănunt = dant, Pac., Naev., and Caecil. ap. ; ; et saep.; cf. Paul. ex Müll.—
Subj.: duim = dem,; : duis,; : duas = des,; ; an old formula in : duit,; ; an old formula in : duint,; ; ; ; —Imper.: DVITOR, XII. Tab. ap. ex conject.—Inf.: DASI = dari, acc. to Paul. ex Müll.: dane = dasne,.—The pres. pass., first pers., dor, does not occur), v. a.
Sanscr. dā, da-dā-mi, give; Gr. δί-δω-μι, δωτήρ, δόσις; cf.: dos, donum, damnum
, to give; and hence, with the greatest variety of application, passing over into the senses of its compounds, derivatives, and synonyms (edere, tradere, dedere; reddere, donare, largiri, concedere, exhibere, porrigere, praestare, impertire, suppeditare, ministrare, subministrare, praebere, tribuere, offerre, etc.), as, to give away, grant, concede, allow, permit; give up, yield, resign; bestow, present, confer, furnish, afford; offer, etc. (very freq.).
In gen.: eam carnem victoribus danunt, Naev. ap. Non. l. l.: ea dona, quae illic Amphitruoni sunt data,; cf.: patera, quae dono mi illic data'st,: dandis recipiendisque meritis,; cf.: ut par sit ratio acceptorum et datorum,: ut obsides accipere non dare consuerint, 1, 4 fin.: obsides,; 1, 31, 7 et saep.: patriam (sc. mundum) dii nobis communem secum dederunt,: hominibus animus datus est ex illis sempiternis ignibus,; cf. : ea dant magistratus magis, quae etiamsi nolint, danda sint,; cf. imperia,: centuria, ad summum usum urbis fabris tignariis data,: Lycurgus agros locupletium plebi, ut servitio, colendos dedit,fin.: ei filiam suam in matrimonium dat,: litteras ad te numquam habui cui darem, quin dederim,: litteras (ad aliquem), to write to one, saep.; cf. ; and in the same signif.: aliquid ad aliquem,fin.: litteras alicui, said of the writer,to give one a letter to deliver,fin.; of the bearer, rarely,to deliver a letter to one,init.: colloquium dare, to join in a conference, converse (poet.), (Lachm.; al. videmus): colloquiumque sua fretus ab urbe dedit,parley, challenge,: dare poenas,to give satisfaction, to suffer punishment,: alicui poenas dare,to make atonement to any one; to suffer for any thing,; ; v. poena: decus sibi datum esse justitia regis existimabant,: quoniam me quodammodo invitas et tui spem das,: dabant hae feriae tibi opportunam sane facultatem ad explicandas tuas litteras,; cf.: ansas alicui ad reprehendendum,: multas causas suspicionum offensionumque,: facultatem per provinciam itineris faciundi,; for which: iter alicui per provinciam,; ; : modicam libertatem populo,: consilium,: praecepta,fin.: tempus alicui, ut, etc.,: inter se fidem et jusjurandum,: operam,to bestow labor and pains on any thing,: operam virtuti,; also: operam, ne,: veniam amicitiae,: vela (ventis),to set sail,: dextra vela dare,to steer towards the right,: me librum L. Cossinio ad te perferendum dedisse,: sin homo amens diripiendam urbem daturus est, et saep.: ita dat se res, so it is circumstanced, so it is, Poëta ap. ; cf.: prout tempus ac res se daret, et saep.— Impers.: sic datur, so it goes, such is fate, i. e. you have your reward, ; ; ; ; .—Part. perf. sometimes (mostly in poets) subst.: dăta, ōrum, n., gifts, presents, ; (4, 14, 6 M.); (but not in , where dona data belong together, as in the archaic formula in : DATVM DONVM DVIT, P. R. Q.).— Prov.: dantur opes nulli nunc nisi divitibus,; cf.: dat census honores,.—
Poet. with inf.: da mihi frui perpetuā virginitate,allow me,; : di tibi dent captā classem reducere Trojā,; so ; ; et saep.—
With ne: da, femina ne sim,.
In partic.
In milit. lang.
Nomina, to enroll one's self for military service, to enlist, ; ; ; cf. transf. beyond the military sphere,.—
Manus (lit., as a prisoner of war, to stretch forth the hands to be fettered; cf. ; hence),to yield, surrender,; and more freq. transf. beyond the milit. sphere,to yield, acquiesce,; ; ; ; ; ; ; —
Terga, for the usual vertere terga; v. tergum.—
To grant, consent, permit.
Esp. in jurid. lang.: DO, DICO, ADDICO, the words employed by the praetor in the execution of his office; viz. DO in the granting of judges, actions, exceptions, etc.; DICO in pronouncing sentence of judgment; ADDICO in adjudging the property in dispute to one or the other party; cf. Müll.; hence called tria verba,.—
Datur, it is permitted, allowed, granted; with subj. clause: quaesitis diu terris, ubi sistere detur, : interim tamen recedere sensim datur,: ex quo intellegi datur, etc.,.—
In philos. lang., to grant a proposition: in geometria prima si dederis, danda sunt omnia: dato hoc, dandum erit illud (followed by concede, etc.),; ; —
Designating the limit, to put, place, carry somewhere; and with se, to betake one's self somewhere: tum genu ad terram dabo,to throw,; cf.: aliquem ad terram,; : me haec deambulatio ad languorem dedit!has fatigued me,: hanc mihi in manum dat,: praecipitem me in pistrinum dabit,: hostes in fugam,: hostem in conspectum,to bring to view,: aliquem in vincula,to cast into prison,; cf.: arma in profluentes,: aliquem usque Sicanium fretum,: aliquem leto,to put to death, to kill,: se in viam,to set out on a journey,: sese in fugam,; cf.: se fugae,: Socrates, quam se cumque in partem dedisset, omnium fuit facile princeps, et saep.—
Designating the effect, to cause, make, bring about, inflict, impose: qui dederit damnum aut malum,: nec consulto alteri damnum dari sine dolo malo potest,; ; cf.: malum dare,: hoc quī occultari facilius credas dabo,: inania duro vulnera dat ferro,: morsus,; cf.: motus dare,to impart motion, (but motus dare, to make motion, to move, be moved, ): stragem,: equitum ruinas,to overthrow,.—With part. fut. pass.: pectora tristitiae dissolvenda dedit,caused to be delivered from sadness,.— Prov.: dant animos vina,. —
Aliquid alicui, to do any thing for the sake of another; to please or humor another; to give up, sacrifice any thing to another (for the more usual condonare): da hoc illi mortuae, da ceteris amicis ac familiaribus, da patriae, Sulp. ap. : aliquid auribus alicujus, Trebon. : Caere hospitio Vestalium cultisque diis,: plus stomacho quam consilio, et saep.: ut concessisti illum senatui, sic da hunc populo,i. e. forgive him, for the sake of the people,: dabat et famae, ut, etc.,.—Hence,
Se alicui, to give one's self up wholly, to devote, dedicate one's self to a person or thing, to serve: dedit se etiam regibus,; so ; ; Poëta ap. ; ; ; : mihi si large volantis ungula se det equi,; ; ; ; cf. : se et hominibus Pythagoreis et studiis illis,: se sermonibus vulgi,: se jucunditati,: se populo ac coronae,to present one's self, appear,; cf.: se convivio, et saep.: si se dant (judices) et sua sponte quo impellimus inclinant,.—
Of discourse, to announce, tell, relate, communicate (like accipere, for to learn, to hear, v. accipio, II.; mostly ante-class. and poet.): erili filio hanc fabricam dabo,: quam ob rem has partes didicerim, paucis dabo,; cf. : imo etiam dabo, quo magis credas,: da mihi nunc, satisne probas?: Thessalici da bella ducis,: is datus erat locus colloquio,appointed,: fixa canens ... Saepe dedit sedem notas mutantibus urbes,i. e. foretold, promised,.—In pass., poet. i. q.: narratur, dicitur, fertur, etc., is said: seu pius Aeneas eripuisse datur,; ; .—
Fabulam, to exhibit, produce a play (said of the author; cf.: docere fabulam, agere fabulam),; ; ; ; ; Don.; and transf.,; cf. also: dare foras librum = edere,.—
Verba (alicui), to give

empty words, i. e. to deceive, cheat, ; ; ; Ruhnk.; Quadrig. ap. ; ; A.; ; ; et saep.—

Alicui aliquid (laudi, crimini, vitio, etc.), to impute, assign, ascribe, attribute a thing to any one, as a merit, a crime, a fault, etc.: nunc quam rem vitio dent, quaeso animum attendite,: hoc vitio datur,: inopiā criminum summam laudem Sex. Roscio vitio et culpae dedisse,; ; ; ; et saep.—
Alicui cenam, epulas, etc., to give one a dinner, entertain at table (freq.): qui cenam parasitis dabit,; ; ; ; ; : prandium dare,; cf. ; —
To grant, allow, in gen. (rare, but freq. as impers.; v. B. 2. supra): dari sibi diem postulabat,a respite,.

la:conj:donec.html:
dōnĕc,
conj. [shortened from ante- and post-class. form dōnĭcum, from old dative doni (dioni; for root, etc., v. dies) and conj. cum; prop. at the time of day when; form donicum, Liv. And., Cato and Plaut. ap. P.; ; ; ; ; ; . 2, 34; ; ; Fragm. ap. P.; .—In the Inscr. of Orell. 4370 DONIQVIES is i. q. DONIQUE IS, and donique = donicum; so, donique,; Lachm.].—Donec denotes the relation of two actions in time,
As contemporaneous, as long as, while, during the time in which; or,
As in immediate succession, until, up to the time at which (synonymous with dum, I. B. and II.—in the ante-class. and postAug. periods freq.; four times in Cic. only in signif. II. with indic.; not in Caes.).
As long as, while (so perh. not till the Aug. period).
With indic.: neque dulces amores Sperne, puer, Donec virenti canities abest,: donec gratus eram tibi, etc. ... Persarum vigui rege beatior ... Donec non alia magis Arsisti, etc. ... Romanà vigui clarior Iliā,, and 5; ; ; ; ; ; ; : donec eris felix, multos numerabis amicos,.—
With subj.: (elephanti) nihil sane trepidabant, donec continenti velut ponte agerentur,; : edixit ne quis militis, donec in castris esset, bona possideret, etc.,; ; ; 21, 10; 25, 11; ;
Until, till at length (so in all periods).
With indic. (cf. Zumpt, Gr. § 575): ne quoquam exurgatis, donec a me erit signum datum,: haud desinam, donec perfecero hoc,; cf. : neque tamen finis . . . fiebat, donec populus senatum coëgit, etc.,; : hic regnabitur ... donec regina sacerdos geminam partu dabit Ilia prolem,; et saep.: neque credebam Donec Sosia fecit sibi uti crederem,.—So with perf., ; Liv. praef. 3, 48; 23, 31; ; ; ; ; et saep.: me attrectare nefas, donec me flumine vivo abluero,: socii consurgere tonsis ... Donec rostra tenent siccum, etc.,; cf. ; ; —
With subj.: Actia pugna refertur, donec alterutrum velox Victoria fronde coronet,.—So in the praes., ; ; ; ; —In the imperf., ; ; ; ; : trepidationis aliquantum edebant, donec quietem ipse timor fecisset,—So with pluperf., —
Ellipt. without a verb: neque quisquam hominem conspicatu'st donec in navi super,; cf. in foll. b.
.—
With usque, usque adeo, usque eo, eo usque, in tantum.
With indic.: ibo odorans usque donec persecutus volpem ero vestigiis,; ; : id. aliquoties in die facito usque adeo donec sal desiverit tabescere biduum,; so § 2; ; : usque eo timui, ne, etc. ... donec ad reiciendos judices venimus,: eo usque me vivere vultis, donec haud ambiguum regem mea morte faciam,: (humum) in tantum deprimere, donec altitudinis mensuram datam ceperit,.—
With subj.: usque Sessuri, donec cantor "Vos plaudite" dicat,: ni istunc invitassitis Usque adeo, donec, qua domum abeat nesciat, Peristis ambo,: nec eo usque trahatur spiritus donec deficiat,.—

.—
With negatives, donec often limits the time within which something is done or to be done, without implying that it is done or to be done after the limit; Engl., till, before, within a certain time: moveri vetuisse puerum, donec experrectus sit,; : si respexis, donicum ego te jussero, te dedam, etc.,; ; .
